Play the widget below and listen. The note climbs, step after step, for as long as you let it run,
yet it never gets any higher. This is a **Shepard tone**, named after the psychologist Roger Shepard,
who wrote about it in 1964. The BBC once called it "a musical barber's pole": the stripes keep
rising, and the pole stays where it is.

**How to use the page.** Play the first widget, then read how it works and try the *Flat* loudness
curve to see the trick. The second widget is a listening test you can do with a partner.

## Hear it

<div class="sk" data-w="shepard" data-preset="Endless staircase"></div>

- **Motion**: *Steps* is the **Shepard scale**, one semitone at a time. *Glide* is the continuous
  version made later by the composer Jean-Claude Risset, called the **Shepard–Risset glissando**.
- **Direction**: up, down, or hold still. Holding still shows that it is only one chord, really.
- **Octaves in the stack**: how many sine waves are sounding.

## How the trick works

A Shepard tone is not one note but a stack of **sine waves exactly an octave apart**: a C1, C2, C3,
C4 and so on, all sounding together. Your ear hears the stack as one note, C.

Now move every sine wave up one semitone, together. The note is now C♯. Keep going. After twelve
steps each sine wave has gone up an octave, so the stack is back where it started, a pile of Cs. The
note has gone up twelve times and arrived where it began.

What stops you from noticing is the **loudness curve**. It stays still while the sine waves move
through it. It is a bell shape across the frequency range: sine waves near the middle are loud, those
near the very bottom and very top are almost silent. So the highest sine wave fades out as it climbs,
and at the same moment a new, quiet one fades in at the bottom. You never hear one leave or one
arrive. In the plot, each bar is one sine wave and its height is how loud it is.

**Give the trick away.** Choose the preset *Give it away* (or set **Loudness curve** to *Flat*). Now
every sine wave is equally loud, and every octave you hear the top one vanish and a bass note appear
from nowhere. Switch back to *Bell* and the join disappears.

Shepard found that the exact shape does not matter much: almost any smooth curve that tapers off to
silence at the low and high ends works as well as the bell he used. Short gaps between the steps are
said to make the illusion stronger than notes that run together. Compare *Steps* and *Glide* to see
which fools you more.

## Which way did it go? The tritone paradox

Play two Shepard tones **half an octave apart** (a tritone, such as C then F♯). Going up six
semitones and going down six semitones land on the same note, so the pair could be heard either way.
Shepard expected the pair to flip, like an optical illusion that switches as you stare at it.

In 1986 the music psychologist **Diana Deutsch** found something stranger. Each listener tends to hear
the same pairs the same way: one person hears C → F♯ go up and G → C♯ go down, while someone else
hears the opposite. What decides it is *which notes* are played, and the answer seems to depend
partly on the language or dialect a person grew up speaking. Listeners from the south of England and
from California, for example, tended to hear them in opposite ways.

<div class="sk" data-w="tritone"></div>

Answer at least a dozen pairs. Each note on the circle is coloured by what you heard when the pair
**started** on it. Many listeners find the circle splits into two halves: one half heard going up,
the other going down. Compare your circle with a classmate's.

## Where you've heard it

- **Pink Floyd, "Echoes"** (*Meddle*, 1971): the ending rises as a Shepard tone, made by feeding back
  between two tape recorders sharing one tape.
- **The THX "Deep Note"** (introduced 1983), the sound before films in THX cinemas, uses one in its
  opening.
- **Super Mario 64** (1996): the music on the endless staircase in Peach's Castle uses a slightly
  changed Shepard scale, a sound that never ends for stairs that never end.
- **Christopher Nolan's films**: in *The Dark Knight* (2008) the Batpod's engine was a Shepard tone, so
  it seemed to speed up forever instead of changing gear. *Dunkirk* (2017) uses one to make the tension
  feel as if it is always rising.
- **Franz Ferdinand, "Always Ascending"** (2018): a rising Shepard tone runs through the whole song.
- **Composers** have used it too: James Tenney's *For Ann (rising)* is made entirely of a
  slowly changing Shepard glissando, and the end of Karlheinz Stockhausen's *Hymnen* has several falling ones.

The "riser" in dance music, the sweep that builds before a drop, uses the same idea: press *Riser*
in the widget.

## Try this

1. Run *Endless staircase* for a full minute. Stop it and hum the last note. Is it higher than the
   first note? Now play a C on a piano: is your hum near it?
2. Set **Octaves in the stack** to 3. Does the illusion still work? What about 10?
3. With *Glide* and a slow speed, try to follow one sine wave in the plot with your ear. Can you hear
   it fade out at the top?
4. Make a 20-second riser for a song in your DAW: a Shepard glide under a drum fill. Where should it
   stop?

**For students**

"Shepard tone." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepard_tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepard_tone). Named after Roger Shepard (JASA, December 1964); sine waves separated by octaves under a raised-cosine loudness curve; any smooth tapering curve works as well (Shepard); short gaps make it more convincing [citation needed on the page]; 'a musical barber's pole' (BBC Bang Goes the Theory); Risset's continuous version; examples: Echoes (Meddle, 1971), THX Deep Note (1983), Super Mario 64 (1996), The Dark Knight (2008) Batpod, Dunkirk (2017), Always Ascending (2018), Tenney For Ann (rising), Stockhausen Hymnen.

"Tritone paradox." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritone_paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritone_paradox). Pairs of Shepard tones a tritone apart heard as ascending by some and descending by others; Shepard (1963) expected an ambiguous, Necker-cube-like figure; Diana Deutsch (1986) found judgments depend on the tones' positions on the pitch-class circle, and vary with language or dialect (south of England vs California).

**For teachers**

"Jean-Claude Risset." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Risset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Risset). French composer, computer-music pioneer (1938-2016); created the continuous Risset scale (Shepard-Risset glissando) after Shepard's discrete scale.
:::
